teaser: A man wakes to find death crouching on him. The city of Geneva pulled the picture off the wall.
review_notes:
Hodler's family deaths (father 1860, mother 1867, all siblings by 1885, tuberculosis) and his remark about a 'general dying' in the family are paraphrased.
Bertha Stucki (married 1889, divorced 1891) and Augustine Dupin (mother of his son Hector, born 1887) are said to have posed for female figures; exact identification of which figure is which is not given in the lesson.
Removal from the Geneva municipal exhibition in February 1891 on the order of the city authorities; private showing with a one-franc entrance fee earning roughly 1,300 francs: verify figures.
Shown at the Salon du Champ-de-Mars, Paris, 1891, and praised by Puvis de Chavannes.
Inscription on the frame about those who lie down at night and do not wake: paraphrased.
Size about 116 x 299 cm. Bought by the canton of Bern in 1901.
The image used is a rather saturated reproduction.

lesson.text: In 1890 Ferdinand Hodler was 37, living in Geneva, and close to broke. He painted signs and entered every competition with prize money. He had a three-year-old son with one woman, Augustine Dupin, and had just married another, Bertha Stucki, in a marriage that would be over within two years.

Above all, he was afraid. Tuberculosis had killed his father, then his mother, then every one of his brothers and sisters. By his early thirties he was the last of the family. He once said that in his home there had been a general dying, as if a dead person was always in the house.

So he put everything on one canvas three meters wide (116 by 299 cm, about 4 by 10 feet): his fear, the two women in his life, and himself. He painted sleepers stretched on bare ground under dark blankets. Six of them rest peacefully. The seventh does not.
Only one person in this picture has his eyes open. Find him.

spots.title: The man who wakes
spots.text: In the center a bearded man jerks his head up, eyes wide. The face is Hodler's own. He has woken to find something sitting on him.

lesson.text: The something is a figure wrapped head to foot in black cloth, crouched between his legs. It has no visible face. The man pushes at it with both hands, and you can see every muscle in his arms tighten. Hodler drew this body from life with a hard, sculptural outline, the way he had been trained.
On the original frame Hodler wrote a sentence in French. It says, roughly, that more than one person who lies down calmly in the evening will not wake up the next morning.

The black shape is death, then, or the terror of it arriving at night. But notice how Hodler arranges the people around the nightmare. They do not form a natural scene. They are laid out in rows, almost like a pattern.
Trace the layout of the sleepers.

lines.label: Upper row
lines.text: A couple on the left and a lone man on the right lie at the same height, bodies stretched sideways. Pale skin, dark cloth, pale ground: the same three tones repeat.

lines.label: Lower row
lines.text: A second band of sleepers runs along the bottom: one curled figure on the left, an entwined couple on the right. The horizontal bodies say rest, stillness, calm.

lines.label: The black mass
lines.text: In the middle of all those horizontals rises one dark upright block. It breaks the pattern the way a scream breaks silence.

lesson.text: Hodler later gave this method a name: Parallelism. He meant the repetition of similar shapes, side by side, to make a feeling stronger, the way a row of identical trees or a chorus of voices impresses you more than one. Night is the first painting where he tried it fully.

He submitted the canvas to Geneva's city exhibition in February 1891. Days before the opening, the city authorities had it taken down. Naked couples lying together were judged indecent. The dying, apparently, bothered nobody.

Hodler answered by renting a hall nearby and charging one franc at the door to see the banned picture. The scandal did the advertising. He earned well over a thousand francs, enough to ship the huge canvas to Paris.

In Paris it hung in a major exhibition that same year, and one of the organizers singled it out for praise: Pierre Puvis de Chavannes, the grand old man of French mural painting. For a struggling Swiss painter, that approval was a turning point. Invitations from Munich, Berlin and Vienna followed.
Night turned a private fear into a formal design. The rows of calm sleepers are what make the single waking man so frightening.

quiz.question: Whose face did Hodler give the terrified man in the center?
quiz.explanation: The waking man is a self-portrait.

quiz.question: Why did Geneva remove the painting from its exhibition in 1891?
options: The nude couples were judged indecent
It was too large for the room
quiz.explanation: The authorities objected to naked couples lying together.

quiz.question: What did Hodler do after the ban?
options: He repainted the figures with clothes
He showed it in a rented hall for one franc a visit
quiz.explanation: The private showing paid for the picture's trip to Paris.

quiz.question: What does Hodler's term Parallelism mean?
options: Painting two canvases at the same time
Repeating similar shapes side by side to strengthen a feeling
quiz.explanation: He repeated similar forms, here rows of sleepers, to intensify the mood.

quiz.question: Which French painter praised Night in Paris?
quiz.explanation: Puvis de Chavannes singled it out for praise.

facts.text: Hodler lost his parents and all his siblings to tuberculosis.
facts.explanation: By his early thirties he was the last survivor of his family.

facts.text: Every figure in Night is asleep.
facts.explanation: The man in the center has woken in terror.

facts.text: The black figure in the center has a clearly painted face.
facts.explanation: It is wrapped entirely in black cloth, with no visible face.
